card.band: 4 h. A hard long tail: LB25 numerics, LB30, emoji and regional indicators. A frontier agent usually passes most of the file and sometimes everything. Buckets: rule groups, class resolution, random strings. A weaker model gets the basic pair table but misses the numeric and context rules.
card.cheat: The test file lines are not in the image except the visible slice, and the random generator produces unseen strings, so a lookup table fails. The image ships no segmenter or ICU library.
card.grading: Visible: about 10% of LineBreakTest. Hidden: the other roughly 17k cases of LineBreakTest.txt (19,346 total) plus random strings from a sealed generator, compared with a sealed reference built from the same data. Exact opportunity-position match; score is the fraction passed.
card.reference: Reference implemented from the spec and validated against the test file (all cases pass); ICU4X (Unicode-3.0) is used only offline for cross-checks. It scores 1.
card.task: /app ships the UCD property files (LineBreak, EastAsianWidth, emoji-data, general category) and an empty library with a CLI taking a string and printing break opportunities. Agent implements the full UAX #14 pair-table and rule set LB1-LB31, including LB30 East Asian width handling, the quotation, numeric and emoji rules, and the resolution of AI/SG/XX/SA/CJ classes.

Build.why: Sealed reference is a few hundred lines plus table generation; estimated 2-5 days.

spike_plan.kill_if: Pair-only breaker already passes over 85% (too easy, K8) or the full rule set cannot pass 90% of lines after reasonable effort (K9), or ICU and the test file disagree on 18.0 (K4).
spike_plan.pass_if: Basic pair-only breaker passes roughly 30-60% of lines and full rules reach 95%+, showing a partial-credit curve and a weaker-model gap.
steps: Fetch LineBreak.txt and auxiliary/LineBreakTest.txt (18.0.0) into a scratch dir; confirm LineBreakTest header and count test lines.
Write a throwaway Python line breaker from LineBreak.txt with only pair-table rules (LB1, LB2, LB6-LB18, LB31); run it against the test file and record the pass fraction per line.
Add LB25 numerics, LB30/30a/30b and class resolution (AI/SG/XX/SA/CJ) as a second pass; record pass fraction again.
Build an ICU-based oracle on a network host using a unstable/18-compatible segmenter or PyICU, and check it against the test file to confirm the cross-check path matches Unicode 18.0 behaviour.
Run the same test file twice to confirm determinism and that the visible ~10% slice is a stable subset.

v1.summary: The core data is real and verifiable: UCD 18.0.0 exists with LineBreak.txt and auxiliary/LineBreakTest.txt, which is licensed under Unicode License v3, and UAX #14 rev 57 covers Unicode 18.0. Three seed claims fail or need caution: LineBreakTest.txt is under auxiliary/, the 19,346 count is unverified, and ICU4X's stable API targets UCD 15.1, so the cross-check path needs an 18-compatible oracle; the main open risk is K8 (frontier may sit near the reference), which the spike must measure.

v2.note: The source is solid: UCD 18.0.0 and LineBreakTest are confirmed, though the file is under auxiliary/, not the ucd/ root. The 19,346 line count was not verified. The ICU4X cross-check for 18.0 was contradicted, so the random-string oracle depends only on our own reference. Implementing UAX #14 is one well-known algorithm of about 600-800 lines plus table generation. Implementations are common (unicode-linebreak, ICU) and frontier models know the rules well, so a frontier agent at 4 h would likely land near the reference. That is at or below the DeepSWE calibration, so this is too easy. It also overlaps S-im-054 (0.44). It may be worth reviving only as one part of a combined UAX #14/#29/#9 text-algorithm suite.
